messages.subject: Re: [aroma.affymetrix] Non-positive probe signals after calibration/normalization (Was: Re: Some questions about plotting and normalization)
parts:
Hi Jeremy.

On 9/2/07, Jeremy Silver <sil...@wehi.edu.au> wrote:
>
> Hi Henrik,
>
> I've been successfully running the allelic cross-talk calibration,
> however it returns negative estimates of probe signals in a
> substantial proportion of probes (~10% in the example I was looking
> at). The log-additive model of RMA can't deal with negative intensity
> estimates. In all your examples (except the one illustrating MbeiPlm),
> you've used RMA as the probe-summarization method.

Yes, you/we should indeed expect non-positive (non-negative + zero)
signals when we calibrate from allelic crosstalk. In the perfect
world without noise, the calibrated PMB signals of truly AA SNPs
should be all zero, and vice versa for BB SNPs. With symmetric noise,
it is not surprising that we get both positive and negative signals in
the end.

Yes, the log-additive model is not ideal for non-positive signals
since they all become non-defined (missing values) on the log scale.
Here is when total-copy number analysis comes to a rescue. If we only
do total-copy number analysis, we don't care how much A or B we've
got, so we simply sum up the PMA+PMB probe pairs, i.e.

plm <- RmaCnPlm(cs, combineAlleles=TRUE);

This will solve the problem with non-positive signals that are due to
homozygote SNPs. Thus, if you sum PM=PMA+PMB (*), you should see that
the fraction of non-positive signals goes down substantially.

However, even after summing, some of the PMs (*) may still be
non-positive. In the perfect world without noise, this only makes
sense if there is no DNA target for that SNP. We know this is the
case when the true copy-number is zero. It may also be the case for
mis-annotated probes. For all other cases, the only rational is that
there is noise added (and/or that the offset estimate in the allelic
calibration is non-perfect).

So, how do we deal with remaining non-positive PMs (*)? One way to
handle those is simply to discard them *across all chips* like they
never existed, and hope there are enough of positive probes in the
probe set to fit the model. This chance for this "hope" to be true,
increases if we don't stratify by strand, but fit sense and anti-sense
probes together. That is, now we've got:

plm <- RmaCnPlm(cs, mergeStrands=TRUE, combineAlleles=TRUE);
plm$treatNAsAs <- "NA";

The last line (non-documented) tells aroma.affymetrix to exclude a
probe across arrays if one or more of them are missing (after the log
transform). So, instead of looking at the fraction of non-positive
probe signals, see how many of your units contain all non-positive
signals (for which we then would get non-defined chip effect
estimates). Typically this fraction is much smaller.

Even better though, is to only discard single probes, not across
chips. In order to do this, we can estimate the log-additive model
using a weighted approach where we give weights to each data point
(probe). We give all non-positive data points zero weight and all
other equal weight. Ben Bolstad was kind enough to add support for
weights to 'affyPLM' some time ago. Potentially weights can be used
in other ways too, e.g. spatial quality scores etc. Here is how you
fit the log-additive model with non-positive probe signals given
weight zero:

plm <- RmaCnPlm(cs, mergeStrands=TRUE, combineAlleles=TRUE, tags=c("*", "w"));
plm$treatNAsAs <- "weighted";

Eventually this will be the default settings, but until I've had time
to test it thoroughly (I've used it for a long time, but it should
still be validated, benchmarked etc.). The tag "*" expands to the
default for the model class and the give arguments; in this case we
get "RMA,A+B,w".

Ok, what about those units/probe sets for which all probes are
non-positive? This is trickier. It comes down to several things.
Could they be true zeros, which we cannot model with a log-additive
model anyway, i.e. is the problem due to an invalid model instead of
due to how you calibrated? If you think you correct for too much
offset in the calibration, or you for other reason accept having a bit
of positive offset in you PM (*) signals, you can shift the signals
before fitting the model using a global constant. You can do this as:

plm <- RmaCnPlm(cs, mergeStrands=TRUE, combineAlleles=TRUE,

tags=c("+300", "*", "w"));
plm$treatNAsAs <- "weighted";
plm$shift <- +300;

You can always set a shift that makes all your PMs (*) become
positive. This is indeed what most scanner companies, including
Affymetrix, do to the signals you observe in the first place.

The more shift you add the more bias you will get in you raw CNs,
especially for those in the lower intensity range.

>
> If we apply the cross-talk calibration, should we also use MBEI to get
> probe-level summaries (since it can handle negative intensity
> estimates)? I'm guessing that CRMA, when released will deal with this
> - so I suppose that this is an interim question.

Yes, the multiplicative model (MbeiModel) handles non-positive signals
much better than the log-additive. Under certain assumptions about
the error terms the two models are actually identical. However, we've
done ROC evaluations using either model, and the log-additive model
comes out better. However 2, this might be due to a non-optimal
implementation of the multiplicative model, and not due to a weaker
model. It has a lot to do with how you robustify the algorithm and
how you deal with heteroscedasticy. Much more effort for dealing with
this has been put into the log-additive model (affyPLM) compare with
the multiplicative model (affy::fit.li.wong).

Hope this helps

Henrik
